## Analysis

**The financial arithmetic first**

Both courses begin by paying £260,000 for the fit-out. After that:

| | WESTERGATE | PENDLARROW |
|---|---|---|
| Deposit remaining after fit-out | £50,000 | £50,000 |
| Vehicle | — | −£34,000 |
| Deposit remaining after both | £50,000 | £16,000 |
| Annual Ardgowrie revenue | — | +£118,000 |
| Farm vet cost (incl. on-costs) | — | −£71,000 |
| Vehicle running (est.) | — | −£6,000 |
| Net annual contribution, Ardgowrie | — | ~£41,000 |
| Grant post April 2027 | — | +£100,000 |

Over four years to 2030-04-30 when the clawback obligation expires, PENDLARROW generates roughly £164,000 net from Ardgowrie operations plus the £100,000 grant, against the £34,000 vehicle capital outlay — a net advantage over WESTERGATE of around £230,000. On a straight-line financial read, PENDLARROW wins by a large margin.

Even in surrender scenarios the arithmetic is less bad than it looks. If the contract is eventually given back, the grant is repaid in full but was received in full — the grant element nets to zero, not a loss. The operating contribution from however many years the contract was held still accrues (£41,000 × years held), and the vehicle is recoverable on resale. PENDLARROW is materially worse than WESTERGATE financially only if the contract is surrendered within the first few months, before operating contribution covers the vehicle cost.

**The cash position**

£16,000 on deposit after fit-out and vehicle, with a £1.84m annual turnover business generating meaningful monthly operating cash flow, is tight but probably survivable. Ardgowrie revenue starts November 2026 and the grant arrives post-April 2027 — the exposed window is roughly six months. In WESTERGATE the cushion is £50,000, which is still thin for a practice this size but more comfortable. Neither course is flush.

**The grant threshold question**

The grant requires farm and equine to be at least 30 per cent of turnover at the April 2027 assessment. The problem presents the qualifying calculation as £622,000 / £1,958,000 = 31.8 per cent, using last year's base (year to March 2026) plus the annualised Ardgowrie contract.

There is a genuine question about methodology. "Annualised value of work in force on that date" might instead mean the current run rate at April 2027. If so, small animal will have grown approximately 13 months at 11 per cent from the March 2026 base:

£1,336,000 × 1.11^(13/12) ≈ £1,496,000

Farm and equine at April 2027: £504,000 + £118,000 = £622,000
Total: £622,000 + £1,496,000 = £2,118,000
Ratio: **29.4 per cent** — below the 30 per cent threshold.

If the grant authority applies this methodology, PENDLARROW qualifies for no grant at all. The practice would bear all the operational burden and commitment while receiving nothing. This is not a resolved risk; it is a number that sits just below the line. Before committing to PENDLARROW, the practice should obtain written confirmation of how the assessment denominator is constructed. The problem implies the last-year-plus-new-contract basis is correct, and I will not override that, but the margin is thin enough that this should be verified, not assumed.

**The night call-out problem — the decisive issue**

The outgoing practice surrendered this contract after nine years. Nine years is not a short trial. It represents a substantial investment in the relationship, the knowledge of the farm and the cattle, and presumably multiple attempts to make the rota sustainable. They gave it up anyway. Their stated reason, on the handover call, was the night call-out load on 900 dairy cattle.

Dairy cattle calve around the clock. Night call-out load on a herd of this size is a structural feature, not a remediable operational failing. It was there in year one and it was still there in year nine.

Two facts are offered to mitigate this:

1. *Kirstie Ballantyne-Rowe will move with the contract.* This is the strongest single argument for PENDLARROW. She knows the farm, the herd, the geography, and the call-out pattern. But it also raises the question of why the outgoing practice surrendered the contract if it was an individual vet's willingness that was the constraint — if Kirstie was happy to continue, why did the practice give it up? The most likely answer is that the issue was not Kirstie herself but the wider rota coverage burden on the rest of the practice when she was unavailable, on holiday, or ill. That burden does not move with her.

2. *Wrentham Cross already does farm and equine work (£504,000) and will have existing farm vets who can provide backup.* This is true, and it does reduce the single-point-of-failure risk slightly. But those vets are not idle. Adding 900 dairy cattle to their on-call rota is a material addition to their workload.

Kirstie is a key person risk regardless. If she leaves before 2030-04-30 — burned out, recruited elsewhere, personal reasons — the practice faces an acute choice: find a qualified replacement quickly enough to maintain the herd health contract above 700 cattle, or surrender the contract and repay £100,000. Neither option is straightforward. Finding a farm vet who will take primary call for 900 dairy cattle at £71,000 in a rural area is not a fast hire.

**The clawback as a structural trap**

The grant clawback is the mechanism that turns the night call-out risk from an operational inconvenience into a financial time-bomb. Without the clawback, the calculus is simple: take the contract, earn the operating contribution, accept the night rota burden, and if it becomes unsustainable, hand it back — just as the outgoing practice eventually did. The business case survives.

With the clawback, the exit is locked until 2030-04-30. If the same structural pressure that caused the outgoing practice to surrender in year nine eventually causes Wrentham Cross to surrender in year three or four, the £100,000 that came in goes back out, the operating contribution for those years offsets the vehicle cost but no more, and the practice has spent three or four years under night rota pressure during the critical period of opening and bedding in a new small animal surgery.

The grant is not a subsidy for taking the risk. It is a conditional payment that disappears if the risk materialises in the way it has already demonstrably materialised at the previous holder.

**Strategic direction**

Wrentham Cross is fitting out a new small animal surgery. Small animal is growing 11 per cent a year. Farm and equine is flat. The practice's strategic direction — revealed by its own investment decision — is small animal. The next hire, on WESTERGATE, goes into that growing side. On PENDLARROW, it goes into a sector that has been flat for three years to service a demanding contract in a flat sector so that a grant can subsidise a small animal facility. The two limbs of PENDLARROW are operationally and strategically disconnected, and the management attention required to open Ordsall Green, onboard Ardgowrie, integrate Kirstie, and build a workable night rota is not divisible without cost.

**Verdict**

PENDLARROW has real financial upside and the downside in surrender scenarios is more bounded than it first appears (the grant is symmetric). But the decisive element is the combination of a structural night call-out load with a four-year clawback obligation. The outgoing practice provides direct empirical evidence — nine years of it — that this contract's demands are eventually unsustainable for a multi-discipline practice. The clawback means the grant's financial value exists only if the contract is held exactly through the period during which that sustainability pressure plays out. Taking a £100,000 conditional payment in exchange for bearing an obligation that the previous holder documented as the reason they gave it up, during the same period the practice is opening a new facility that needs management focus, is the wrong trade.

---

READING
  Both courses start by paying the £260,000 fit-out from the £310,000 deposit, leaving £50,000 (WESTERGATE) or £50,000 before the £34,000 vehicle (PENDLARROW, leaving £16,000). The financial case for PENDLARROW is real: Ardgowrie nets roughly £41,000 a year after the farm vet and vehicle running, and the grant adds £100,000 after the April 2027 assessment — a ~£230,000 advantage over four years. Even in surrender scenarios the financial damage is bounded, because the grant clawback is symmetric (received and repaid, net zero) and the operating contribution from however many years the contract is held is positive.

  Three concerns complicate the picture. First, the grant threshold. The qualifying figure of 31.8 per cent uses last year's accounts plus annualised Ardgowrie. If instead the assessment uses the current run rate at April 2027, small animal will have grown roughly 13 months at 11 per cent: approximately £1,496,000. Farm and equine would then be £622,000 of £2,118,000 — 29.4 per cent, below the threshold. PENDLARROW's entire financial logic rests on the 31.8 per cent calculation being correct; the practice should verify the methodology in writing before committing, because the margin is uncomfortably thin.

  Second, the cash position. £16,000 in reserve after fit-out and vehicle is very thin. The existing business generates operating cash flow and Ardgowrie revenue starts November, but this window (November 2026 to April 2027) is the most exposed period while also being the period of opening a new surgery.

  Third, and decisive, is the night call-out issue and its interaction with the clawback. The outgoing practice held this contract for nine years — a long and experienced tenure — and surrendered it specifically because of the night call-out load on 900 dairy cattle. Dairy cattle calving patterns are structural; they do not change between holders. Kirstie moving with the contract is the strongest argument for PENDLARROW: she knows the farm and accepts the workload. But the previous practice's reason for giving it up was most likely the coverage burden on the wider rota when Kirstie was unavailable, not Kirstie's own willingness — and that burden follows the contract, not the vet. Kirstie is also a single point of failure: if she leaves before 2030-04-30, the practice must either find a replacement qualified farm vet quickly (difficult in a rural area) or surrender the contract and repay £100,000.

  The clawback converts what looks like a grant subsidy into a conditional obligation. Without it, if the night rota eventually becomes unsustainable — as it did for the previous holder — the practice gives back the contract, the grant nets to zero, and the operating contribution for the years held offsets the vehicle. With the clawback in place, the practice is locked until 2030. The grant's financial value is conditional on holding the contract through exactly the period during which the structural pressure documented by the outgoing practice plays out.

  WESTERGATE foregoes £100,000 and roughly £160,000 in net operating contribution over four years. That is a real cost. But it eliminates the conditional liability, the clawback exposure, the key-person dependency, and the operational distraction of managing 900 dairy cattle night calls during the critical period of opening Ordsall Green. It also aligns with the direction the practice has already chosen: small animal growth at 11 per cent a year, and a new small animal surgery as the next investment. PENDLARROW takes the practice deeper into a flat sector, with an operationally demanding commitment, to fund a facility in the sector the practice is actually growing. The two limbs pull in opposite directions, and the price of connecting them is taking on precisely what the previous practice found unsustainable and documented as their reason for leaving.

CALL
  WESTERGATE

GROUNDS
  The outgoing practice's explicit, documented reason for surrendering this contract after nine years is the night call-out load — a structural feature of 900 dairy cattle that does not change between holders — and the clawback obligation to 2030-04-30 means the grant's financial benefit exists only if the practice holds the contract through exactly the period during which that same structural pressure is most likely to force the same outcome.
